nodes.summary: The potential-method charge of a queue operation is $2$ for an enqueue and $1$ for a dequeue.
nodes.title: Amortized charge of a queue operation

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$ and value $v$, the contents of the queue obtained by enqueueing $v$ onto $q$ are the contents of $q$ followed by $v$.
nodes.title: Enqueueing appends to the contents

nodes.summary: If dequeueing a queue $q$ succeeds and returns an element $a$ and a queue $r$, then the contents of $q$ are $a$ followed by the contents of $r$.
nodes.title: A successful dequeue splits off the first element

nodes.summary: A queue is stored as a dequeue list and an enqueue list whose most recently enqueued element comes first. Its contents are its elements in FIFO order: the dequeue list followed by the reverse of the enqueue list.
nodes.title: Contents of a two-list queue

nodes.summary: For every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of dequeueing from $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus $1$. This includes the case where $q$ is empty.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of dequeueing

nodes.summary: For a queue stored as an enqueue list and a dequeue list, the modeled cost of dequeueing is $1$ when the dequeue list is nonempty, and $m + 1$ when the dequeue list is empty, where $m$ is the length of the enqueue list (the number of elements reversed when they are moved to the dequeue list).
nodes.title: Modeled cost of a dequeue

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$, dequeueing $q$ returns nothing if and only if the contents of $q$ are empty.
nodes.title: Dequeueing fails exactly on empty queues

nodes.summary: Dequeueing from a two-list queue $q$ returns the next element in first-in, first-out order together with the remaining queue, or returns no element together with $q$ itself when $q$ is empty. In both cases the recorded cost is the modeled dequeue cost of $q$.
nodes.title: Timed dequeue

nodes.summary: For every two-list queue $q$ and every value $v$, the modeled cost of enqueueing $v$ onto $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus $2$.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of enqueueing

nodes.summary: Enqueueing a value $v$ onto a two-list queue $q$ returns the queue obtained from $q$ by adding $v$ at the back, that is, by prepending $v$ to the enqueue list, together with a recorded cost of $1$.
nodes.title: Timed enqueue

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$, the emptiness test of $q$ returns true if and only if the contents of $q$ are empty.
nodes.title: The queue emptiness test matches the contents

nodes.summary: A queue operation over a type $\alpha$ is either a request to enqueue a value $v \in \alpha$ or a request to dequeue. Sequences of such operations are used to state aggregate cost bounds.
nodes.title: Queue operation

nodes.summary: For a queue stored as an enqueue list and a dequeue list, the potential is the length of the enqueue list: the number of elements that will be reversed when they are moved to the dequeue list.
nodes.title: Potential of a two-list queue

nodes.summary: For every list of queue operations and every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of running the operations from left to right starting at $q$, plus the potential of the final queue, equals the potential of $q$ plus the total charge of the operations.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of a sequence of queue operations

nodes.summary: For every list of $n$ queue operations and every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of running the operations from left to right starting at $q$ is at most the potential of $q$ plus $2n$.
nodes.title: Linear bound on the cost of queue operations

nodes.summary: Running a list of queue operations from a queue $q$ performs the operations one step at a time from left to right, starting at $q$. The result is the final queue, and the cost is the sum of the costs of the individual steps; running the empty list returns $q$ at cost $0$.
nodes.title: Running a sequence of queue operations

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$ and every queue operation $o$, the modeled cost of performing $o$ on $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus the charge of $o$.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of one queue operation

nodes.summary: For a queue $q$, an enqueue operation with value $v$ performs the costed enqueue of $v$ onto $q$. A dequeue operation performs the costed dequeue of $q$ and keeps the remaining queue and the cost, discarding the removed value; on an empty queue the remaining queue is $q$ itself.
nodes.title: One step of a queue operation

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$, the array obtained from $q$, read as a list, equals the contents of $q$.
nodes.title: Array conversion lists the contents

nodes.summary: For a list of queue operations, the total charge is the sum of the amortized charges of its operations, where an enqueue is charged $2$ and a dequeue is charged $1$.
nodes.title: Total charge of a sequence of queue operations

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.

breadcrumbs.label: Lists, stacks, queues and dynamic arrays
